item.title: US Government Requests $30.3 Million for AI-Powered Polygraph Modernization
item.description:
US Government Requests $30.3 Million for AI-Powered Polygraph Modernization

The US government has requested $30.3 million over the next five years to develop an improved form of lie detector known as Polygraph+ (or Polygraph Next). The program aims to modernize federal credibility assessment technologies to enhance accuracy and reliability.

🔍 Overview

Managed by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), Polygraph+ will be utilized for the vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” This comes as the Pentagon has increasingly used polygraph tests under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to identify sources of press leaks, including the testing of approximately 50 Joint Staff officers following reports on US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.

🧩 How it works

The program focuses on two primary technical advancements:

  • AI and Machine Learning: The use of scoring algorithms to find patterns in data that human examiners may miss and to create “multi-modal” deception detection by combining multiple measurements into a single score.
  • Standoff Sensing: The ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to the subject.

⚙️ Key details

Following an open submission process by the Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) in 2023, two companies were selected to build prototypes:

Company Capability/Focus
Presage Technologies Measuring heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras
Altec Research Non-contact sensing tracking head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity

💡 Why it matters

Current polygraph technology, largely unchanged since the 1920s, relies on measurements of sweat, breathing, pulse, and blood pressure. However, the technology faces significant criticism:

  • Reliability Issues: In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment found limited evidence supporting its use for employee screening, and in 2003, the US National Research Council called the evidence for its efficacy “weak at best.”
  • Subjectivity and Bias: Interpretations can vary wildly between examiners, and individuals from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive.
  • Countermeasures: Interviewees can beat the test through training, such as using a pin in a shoe to artificially heighten physiological responses.
  • Scale Risks: With 2.8 million employees in the DOD, an imperfect system could result in tens of thousands of false accusations.

Critics such as legal scholar Kyri Kotsoglou describe the effort as “a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” while associate professor Sophie van der Zee notes that while various strategies like brain scans and thermal cameras have been tried, “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose.”

#AI #MachineLearning #Defense #Polygraph #Biometrics

Source: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector

item.title: MIT Technology Review Investigation Finds Failures in Border Surveillance Towers
item.description:
MIT Technology Review Investigation Finds Failures in Border Surveillance Towers

An investigation by MIT Technology Review has documented that over a thousand people died in areas monitored by U.S. southern border surveillance towers without being reached or apprehended.

🔍 Overview

Over the past 25 years, the US has invested billions of dollars into a “virtual wall” of surveillance towers along the southern border. These towers were intended to:

  • Detect border crossers
  • Apprehend border crossers
  • Save lives

⚙️ Key details

Recent updates to the surveillance infrastructure include the installation of AI-powered towers. These specific towers are designed to spot people automatically; however, the investigation found that some individuals who died were under the watch of these AI-powered systems.

#AI #Surveillance #BorderSecurity #MITTechnologyReview

Source: Roundtables: The Deadly Failures of The Virtual Border Wall

item.title: AI Surveillance Towers Deployed for Border Monitoring in Southern California
item.description:
AI Surveillance Towers Deployed for Border Monitoring in Southern California

The U.S. border in Southern California has seen a proliferation of surveillance towers equipped with artificial intelligence designed to track movements and distinguish border-crossers from animals and other people.

🧩 How it works

Contractors have implemented newer camera systems using AI to monitor the border. Key technical capabilities include:

  • Hardware: Towers such as those made by General Dynamics feature two sets of electro-optical and infrared cameras.
  • Range: Long-range lenses are capable of tracking targets 5 to 7 miles away.
  • Network Integration: These towers are part of a broader network including trail cameras, radar, infrared sensors, drones, blimps, and satellites (as directed by the Trump administration in March 2025).

⚙️ Key details

  • Cost: The overall cost of these AI surveillance systems exceeds one billion dollars.
  • Scale: More than 120 surveillance towers are located along the California border.

💡 Why it matters

An analysis by the Times of San Diego and an investigation by MIT Technology Review have examined the effectiveness of these systems in relation to migrant deaths:

  • Analysis: At least 138 cases in the past four years involved migrants’ remains found within the range of the cameras.
  • Visibility: An MIT Technology Review topographical analysis estimated more than half of these remains were located in spots where a camera would have a clear line of sight.
Individual Date Found Location/Context Tower Proximity/Visibility
Graciela Gómez Hernández September 2025 Otay Mountain Wilderness One mile away from a General Dynamics tower
Marcia Dutra July 2023 Next to a border fence Tower 2,000 feet away; out of sight of the slope
Elvi Vasquez Bortolon February 2024 Ridge near border wall Tower 1,400 feet away; hidden by a ridge
Ramón Montenegro August 2024 Mountains near Dulzura Tower 1,300 feet away; invisible on other side of a hill

#AI #Surveillance #ComputerVision #BorderSecurity

Source: She died at the San Diego border. A surveillance camera was in plain sight

item.title: Investigation Finds Over 1,000 Deaths Near US-Mexico Border Surveillance Towers
item.description:
Investigation Finds Over 1,000 Deaths Near US-Mexico Border Surveillance Towers

A 15-month collaboration between MIT Technology Review and Times of San Diego has produced the first comprehensive map and analysis of deaths occurring near US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) surveillance towers along the US-Mexico border.

🔍 Overview

Journalists examined the failures of border surveillance technology and the stories of people who died in the borderlands. The investigation found more than 1,050 people died within range of border surveillance towers between 2015 and early 2026. This includes more than 110 deaths within range of modern autonomous towers from Anduril since 2021.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Scope of Analysis: The study analyzed nearly 600 towers and cases dating back to 2015.
  • Findings: Deaths were found within the advertised range of nearly two-thirds of the analyzed towers.
  • Terrain Analysis: Topographical analysis showed that while some towers have sight of as little as 10% of their advertised area, most deaths did not occur in blind spots.
  • Investment: The US has spent billions on the “virtual wall” and is set to spend $1 billion more to triple its size by 2034.

🧩 Methodology

To build the dataset, investigators merged records from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, No More Deaths, and Humane Borders with records from over a dozen agencies.

  • Texas Data Collection: Because Texas lacks a national protocol or online record-sharing initiative, researchers filed records requests to sheriffs in 17 counties beginning in July 2025.
  • AI Integration: For the high volumes of records received from Hidalgo, Webb, and Kenedy Counties, the team used Anthropic’s Claude via API to inspect case reports and extract coordinates of where remains were found.
  • Verification: A case was considered for analysis if investigators could confirm the person was believed to be crossing the border, where the remains were found, and roughly when they died.

💡 Why it Matters

Despite the use of AI-equipped towers designed to automatically detect and track people, many deaths remain unnoticed by technology:

  • In 2024, 18 people died in one small stretch of desert in range of three Anduril towers.
  • One individual died 360 feet from the closest surveillance tower and was first spotted by landfill employees.
  • Another woman died near an Anduril tower in a location where terrain analysis indicated the tower should have had clear sight; her decomposed body was spotted weeks later by agents.
  • The Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported in 2017 that some data collected by agents was unreliable, citing instances in Texas where agents credited towers for apprehensions in areas where no such towers existed.

#BorderSurveillance #AI #CustomsAndBorderProtection #Anduril #HumanRights

Source: How we made the first comprehensive map of deaths along the US border’s “virtual wall” Source: 4 ways to address the failures we found along the US border’s “virtual wall” Source: The US spent billions on border surveillance. Why can’t it catch people before they die?
